faqs.q: What does it cost to get an animal out of my Queens attic?
faqs.a: It depends on the animal, how it got in, and how much sealing and cleanup the house needs. Our crew inspects first, shows you the entry points, and gives you a quote after inspection before any removal work begins — no prices promised over the phone.

faqs.q: When do animals get into Queens attics most often?
faqs.a: Our crew's Queens work centers on Norway rats along the commercial corridors, raccoons and squirrels off the Forest Park canopy, and pigeons in elevated-train structures and roof bulkheads. The pattern follows the housing and the habitat: flushing bay keeps animals close, and once one finds a way into a roofline, chimney, or crawlspace here, it usually comes back until every entry is sealed. That is why we pair removal with proofing on every Queens job rather than just taking the animal out.

Queens.geographic_features: Flushing Bay (industrial waterfront in the north), Forest Park (large wooded park on the Brooklyn line), Jamaica Bay (marsh and beach at the south), Flushing Meadows Corona Park (parkland and lakes in the center)
Queens.housing_era: Queens mixes attached brick rowhouses in Ridgewood and Astoria, garden apartments in Forest Hills and Jackson Heights, two-family homes across Jamaica and Richmond Hill, and pre-war apartment buildings along the elevated lines. Porches, bulkheads, and shared rooflines are the usual wildlife entries.

Queens.wildlife_intro:
Queens keeps our crew busy with Norway rats along the commercial corridors, raccoons and squirrels off the Forest Park canopy, and pigeons in elevated-train structures and roof bulkheads. Flushing Bay  gives wildlife food, water, and cover within a short run of almost every roof in town, and the housing does the rest — once an animal finds a soft soffit, an uncapped chimney, or a gap at the roofline, it treats the house as part of its territory.

The year has a rhythm in Queens. Fall pushes squirrels, raccoons, and rodents indoors ahead of winter; spring brings denning mothers looking for chimneys and attic corners; summer is when bat colonies are most visible in older homes and when young animals start ranging on their own. Most Queens jobs start with a full roofline and foundation inspection, then removal and sealing every entry we find, because closing only the obvious hole rarely holds.
